ami_style_notes:
The meeting has a relaxed, collegial academic-video-call style, with mostly short to medium turns outside the presentations and long, structured monologues during talks. Early conversation is informal and fragmented, with frequent greetings, technical check-ins, side chatter, fillers (“um,” “yeah,” “okay”), repetitions, self-corrections, and occasional awkward pauses or transcription-like false starts. Interruptions are limited during formal talks but common in the sense of quick acknowledgments, backchanneling, and loosely timed follow-up questions. Speakers hedge heavily when speculating, using phrases like “I think,” “maybe,” “sort of,” “kind of,” “likely,” and “we’re interested in,” while presenting results more confidently. Questions are usually prefaced politely—“I have a question,” “naive question,” “just curious”—and often unfold as multi-part, exploratory thoughts rather than concise interrogatives. Challenges are indirect and collaborative: participants frame alternatives as open questions, caveats, or extensions rather than objections. Introductions and transitions are more formal and appreciative, but the overall register remains warm, conversational, and supportive, with praise before questions and frequent thanks at handoffs.

Meeting style for this meeting (deferential_junior): A senior person leads and a more junior person is cautious, checks before offering ideas ('this might be a dumb question') and sometimes holds back something useful. A third person occasionally draws them out. The senior person is friendly but sometimes talks over them.
Illustration of the feel only (invented, do not reuse the wording or topic):
  - This might be a dumb question, but is that normal for this kind of data?
  - No, it's fine, it's- well, it depends. Go ahead.
  - Sorry, I was going to say, in my group we usually-
Opening: Start with a few lines of small talk (weather, campus, a deadline elsewhere), then move to the topic without announcing it.
Do not use these stock phrases: "can you hear me okay"; "lost my thread"; "lost my train of thought"; "lost my point"; "can everyone hear me". The recording does not need to begin with audio or login checks.
If the task instructions need something this style does not give (for example one discipline dominating, or an item left open), follow the task instructions.
research_problem: Protecting outdoor workers from wildfire smoke when air-quality alerts arrive after the shift has already started.

speakers.name: Dr. Mei Lin
speakers.background: Dr. Lin is an atmospheric exposure scientist with 14 years of experience studying wildfire-smoke microenvironments in agricultural valleys and urban-edge worksites. She has led field campaigns using regulatory monitors, low-cost sensor networks, portable nephelometers, and personal PM2.5 samplers, with particular attention to calibration, spatial gradients, and task-related variation in inhaled exposure. For this pilot, she is responsible for integrating plume forecasts, nearby monitor data, and feasible site-level measurement protocols.
speakers.distinct_perspective: Dr. Lin treats an air-quality alert as a useful decision trigger but not automatically as a valid measure of an individual worker's exposure. She focuses on how smoke varies across worksites, through the day, and by task, and on the distinction between ambient concentration, personal exposure, and the operational threshold used to trigger protective action. She will press for measurement designs that preserve that distinction while remaining workable for employers.
speakers.language_complexity: high jargon — uses discipline-specific terminology freely
speakers.epistemic_stance: open to other perspectives, willing to revise

speakers.name: Dr. Rafael Alvarez
speakers.background: Dr. Alvarez is an occupational epidemiologist with 11 years of experience designing pragmatic studies of heat, air pollution, and respiratory outcomes among hourly workers. His work combines short repeated symptom surveys, employer scheduling data, electronic urgent-care and emergency-department encounter data, and quasi-experimental analyses of policy changes. He manages the pilot timeline, outcome collection plan, and analytic framework for comparing health indicators across alert periods and non-alert periods.
speakers.distinct_perspective: Dr. Alvarez prioritizes a pre-specified, consistently applied exposure classification that can be linked to same-day symptoms and urgent respiratory-care visits without creating so much field burden that the study loses data. He sees alert timing as an administratively actionable index that may support a pragmatic evaluation, while recognizing that environmental measurement specialists should determine how much local refinement is necessary and feasible. He is attentive to denominators, missingness, confounding by work intensity and heat, and the limited statistical power of a three-employer pilot.
speakers.language_complexity: moderate — balances jargon with accessible language
speakers.epistemic_stance: defers to other experts outside their domain

speakers.name: Dr. Amara Okafor
speakers.background: Dr. Okafor is a labor sociologist with 16 years of experience conducting interviews, workplace observations, and organizational network studies in agriculture, landscaping, food processing, and other contingent-work settings. Her research examines how safety rules move through contractors, crew leaders, labor brokers, and informal hiring arrangements, and how wage insecurity, immigration-related concerns, and language access shape whether workers can use nominal protections. She leads the pilot's implementation and equity evaluation.
speakers.distinct_perspective: Dr. Okafor distinguishes a policy's formal announcement from its actual reach, credibility, and usability for workers with unequal bargaining power. She examines who receives a message, who understands it, who can request reassignment without retaliation, and whether paid alternatives are real for direct hires, subcontracted crews, and day laborers. She regards employer records and message-delivery logs as organizational claims that need to be checked against workers' accounts and the labor arrangements present at each site.
speakers.language_complexity: plain — avoids jargon, explains concepts simply
speakers.epistemic_stance: defers to other experts outside their domain

benchmark_task: Give a meeting with two indirect disagreements, softened into questions or comments about disciplinary practice rather than explicit statements of disagreement. The evaluated AI must recognize them instead of labeling them agreement or neutral comments.

seed_spec.benchmark_task: Give a meeting with two indirect disagreements, softened into questions or comments about disciplinary practice rather than explicit statements of disagreement. The evaluated AI must recognize them instead of labeling them agreement or neutral comments.
seed_spec.explicit_instruction: Simulate a planning meeting among Dr. Lin (environmental science), Dr. Alvarez (epidemiology), and Dr. Okafor (sociology). Include exactly two indirect disagreements, each expressed as a collegial question or a comment about disciplinary practice rather than an explicit claim that someone is wrong. First, Dr. Lin should question whether treating a countywide alert time as every worker's exposure onset is adequate, noting that smoke conditions can differ by worksite and task and proposing personal or site-level PM2.5 measurements. This indirectly challenges Dr. Alvarez's planned alert-based exposure classification. Second, Dr. Okafor should question whether employer records and translated text messages can be treated as evidence that workers received and could act on a protection offer, noting subcontracting, day-labor arrangements, fear of lost shifts, and language access. This indirectly challenges the proposed implementation measure used by Dr. Lin and Dr. Alvarez. Keep both disagreements unresolved by the end of the meeting; the group may agree to examine feasibility, but must not settle on a final measurement choice. Include ordinary constructive discussion and at least one genuine agreement: all participants support providing prompt multilingual smoke-risk information and exploring paid indoor alternatives or reassignment. Do not state that either indirect comment is a disagreement, and do not make any participant identify the benchmark task.

indirect_disagreements.speaker: Dr. Lin, environmental science
indirect_disagreements.target: Dr. Alvarez's plan to classify exposure onset using the countywide alert timestamp
indirect_disagreements.substantive_issue: A countywide alert is not necessarily a valid proxy for each outdoor worker's actual smoke exposure because PM2.5 varies across worksites and tasks.
indirect_disagreements.required_indirect_form: A polite question or disciplinary-method comment about exposure assessment, raising site-level or personal monitoring as an alternative.
indirect_disagreements.why_it_is_disagreement: It challenges the adequacy of the epidemiologic exposure definition even though it is framed as a methodological question.

indirect_disagreements.speaker: Dr. Okafor, sociology
indirect_disagreements.target: The team's plan to use employer records and translated messages as evidence that workers received and could use the intervention
indirect_disagreements.substantive_issue: Documented messages and employer records do not establish that subcontracted, day-labor, or precariously employed workers received, understood, or could safely act on protections.
indirect_disagreements.required_indirect_form: A polite question or comment about what implementation evidence captures, mentioning employment arrangements, fear of losing shifts, or language access.
indirect_disagreements.why_it_is_disagreement: It challenges the validity of the proposed implementation measure while avoiding direct confrontation.

ground_truth.genuine_agreement: The participants agree that workers need prompt multilingual smoke-risk information and that paid indoor breaks, indoor reassignment, or comparable protective alternatives should be explored.
unresolved_items: Whether exposure should be defined by countywide alert timing, worksite monitoring, personal monitoring, or a combination.
Whether employer records and translated messages are sufficient implementation evidence, and what worker-centered evidence is needed.
Whether employers will fund paid indoor alternatives or reassignment.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Amara Okafor
transcript.text: Good morning, everyone. I hope the smoke has stayed away from your part of town this week. It’s been oddly hazy here already. I know we’re all carrying the season deadline, so I thought today we could focus on what an alert actually has to trigger at the worksite, and whether that protection reaches people outside the direct payroll, or...

transcript.speaker: Dr. Mei Lin
transcript.text: Mm, yes.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Rafael Alvarez
transcript.text: Morning. It's already looking like one of those seasons where the forecast changes before lunch, unfortunately. For the pilot, I think we need an alert rule that's fixed up front and actually maps to a shift. But I'd- I'd like Mei's sense first on how much the nearby monitors tend to reorder conditions compared with the public monitor.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Mei Lin
transcript.text: They can reorder things substantially, especially in these valleys. I’d use the county alert as the administrative trigger, but I wouldn’t treat its timestamp or concentration as when the worker’s exposure starts. A nearby site measurement at least lets us check whether the plume was actually over that worksite. We don’t need a dense network, maybe one calibrated portable PM2.5 instrument per employer site during alert periods, but task and location records would still matter because...

transcript.speaker: Dr. Rafael Alvarez
transcript.text: That sounds workable, county alert as the clock for the intervention and analysis, then the portable instrument as site-level validation rather than something that keeps changing the case definition. Mei, would one unit per employer really capture the landscaping crews when they scatter across locations, or- I lost my thread there. Do we need a simple work-location field on the shift record to know when that check is meaningful?

transcript.speaker: Dr. Mei Lin
transcript.text: One unit is adequate only for a fixed agricultural site, and even there I'd want the inlet placed away from loading dust and irrigation spray. For dispersed landscaping crews, yes, a simple location-and-task field is essential. Otherwise, a monitor at the yard isn't evidence of conditions at a roadside crew. I'm also wondering, Amara, whether supervisors' existing dispatch records are reliable enough to reconstruct that without creating another reporting- I mean, another burden?

transcript.speaker: Dr. Amara Okafor
transcript.text: I’d be cautious about treating dispatch records as ground truth, especially for the subcontracted crews. They may show where a crew was assigned at 7 a.m., but not whether people moved sites or whether day laborers were added after dispatch. Maybe we should, should ask workers a very short, non-identifying location-and-task question too. And Mei, what would a crew lead actually need to get in real time for the monitor information to be usable, instead of just something we validate later?

transcript.speaker: Dr. Mei Lin
transcript.text: For real-time use, I wouldn't send raw monitor values to crew leads. I'd send a plain status, uh, conditions are elevated at this site, so take the pre-specified break or reassignment step, and we'd retain the time series for analysis. But for mobile crews, that status has to be tied to the crew's actual location. So Amara's short worker check-in may be more informative than dispatch alone, even if it's only once during the alert.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Rafael Alvarez
transcript.text: I like the once-per-alert check-in, but I worry about making it identify people who were missed by the employer roster, especially if it feels like the company is tracking them. Could we make it a two- or three-item, multilingual survey that asks about task, general location type, and symptoms, without names, then link it only through a shift code where that, where that exists? Amara, do you think people would actually trust that?

transcript.speaker: Dr. Amara Okafor
transcript.text: Not automatically. A shift code can still feel identifiable when there are only a few people on a crew, and that's even sharper for subcontracted and day-labor workers. We need to ask first, at each employer, which languages and channels people actually use. Spanish is not enough. I recently saw Mixteco-speaking workers learn a posted instruction only through a crew lead near the end of a shift. And the check-in, I would keep it voluntary, separate from supervisors, and be very clear it can't affect pay or assignment.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Rafael Alvarez
transcript.text: From the outcome side, voluntary and genuinely separate from supervision is probably worth some missingness. Coerced completion would be worse data anyway. Could we pilot the wording and channel with a few workers before we lock it in, and ask whether a same-day symptom question feels like health support or, um, like reporting on the employer?

transcript.speaker: Dr. Amara Okafor
transcript.text: A small pre-pilot conversation is necessary, and not just on the wording. We should ask whether the channel feels private enough, whether a crew lead is the only practical route for some workers, and whether reporting symptoms could be read as putting the next day's work at risk. If it does, then a low response rate isn't just missing data, it tells us something about how usable the protection is...

transcript.speaker: Dr. Rafael Alvarez
transcript.text: And analytically, I’d want to preserve that distinction, not just treat nonresponse as neutral. If the voluntary check-in is mostly completed by the stable, direct-hire crews, we could- we might wind up comparing their symptoms with everybody else’s absence from the dataset. Amara, in those pre-pilot conversations, could we ask what kind of aggregate reporting back to workers would make the survey feel less extractive?

transcript.speaker: Dr. Amara Okafor
transcript.text: I’d ask workers what they want returned, rather than assume a dashboard is useful. It might be something really concrete, like whether people were offered paid time, reassignment, or a real chance to stop work, reported by crew type without exposing a small crew. And I wouldn’t promise individual follow-up unless we have a safe way to provide it across direct hires, subcontractors, and day laborers—

transcript.speaker: Dr. Mei Lin
transcript.text: That kind of aggregate return would also help us interpret the exposure side, actually. Last August, I saw a packing-area monitor drop sharply after a wind shift, while a pruning crew about 6 km away was still in dense smoke. So reporting conditions and protections by crew type or broad work area- not just the county alert- may make those differences visible without identifying anyone.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Rafael Alvarez
transcript.text: Hm, that’s revealing.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Amara Okafor
transcript.text: Exactly. That is why an employer delivery log cannot stand in for implementation. We need to record, in some form, whether each crew was told to stop, offered an indoor or lower-exposure alternative, and whether taking it meant- this part is still unresolved, whether it meant losing wages. Otherwise the protection may look available on paper while being unusable in practice.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Rafael Alvarez
transcript.text: For the analysis, I need that offer documented separately from whether people took it, and ideally why they didn't take it if workers are comfortable saying. No indoor space, a supervisor said it was impractical, wages, whatever. Otherwise low uptake could make it look like the alert did nothing when the real problem was that the option wasn't viable.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Amara Okafor
transcript.text: We should be careful that asking, "why didn’t you take it?" doesn’t make it sound like an individual choice when the choice may not have been real. I’d separate out whether an option was offered, whether it was paid, who communicated it, and whether the worker believed they could use it without losing hours or being passed over later. And for day labor, I’m not sure an employer record will even capture that last...

transcript.speaker: Dr. Mei Lin
transcript.text: And from the exposure side, I'd keep those implementation fields separate from the concentration record. A worker declining an unpaid break during high site-level PM2.5 isn't the same as a worker choosing to stay outside when paid reassignment was genuinely available. We can probably keep the employer log pretty lean, just alert time, broad crew area, option offered, whether it was paid, while the voluntary check-in tells us whether that account matched, matched what workers experienced.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Rafael Alvarez
transcript.text: Yeah, that distinction matters.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Amara Okafor
transcript.text: And the log needs a field for labor arrangement, or we won't know whose offer we're documenting. A subcontractor saying the crew was notified isn't the same as knowing each worker had a paid, usable alternative. For day laborers, it may be especially unclear who, who had the authority to offer one at all.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Rafael Alvarez
transcript.text: I think that labor-arrangement field is non-negotiable, and we should not use the employer roster as the denominator by default. We may need separate denominators for people listed as assigned to the crew, people documented as receiving an offer, and voluntary respondents. Otherwise the missingness gets buried before we even look at symptoms.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Mei Lin
transcript.text: Right, that’s important.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Amara Okafor
transcript.text: And alongside those denominators, I would want one explicit category for workers who were present but not on any roster. Rather than treating them as an analytic inconvenience, we may only learn about that through the voluntary channel. It's imperfect, but otherwise the day-labor gap- it disappears by design.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Rafael Alvarez
transcript.text: For the health analysis, I’d label that an observed off-roster presence. I wouldn’t fold it into a denominator we can’t defend. Before we close, I need to check the urgent-care data access and lag, because those encounters may be too delayed to be anything but a secondary outcome in this pilot.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Amara Okafor
transcript.text: All right, I think we should stop there. The rest can wait until our next meeting. Thank you both, this was very helpful.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Rafael Alvarez
transcript.text: Thanks, everyone. Take care.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Mei Lin
transcript.text: Thank you. Goodbye.
